reason: The provided sources contain over 10 cross-verified claims detailing the launch damage, emergency parasol deployment, and spacewalk repairs that saved Skylab.
story: On May 14, 1973, NASA launched Skylab, America's first space station, aboard a modified Saturn V rocket. But during ascent, severe aerodynamic forces ripped away its micrometeoroid shield, which doubled as a thermal protection barrier. The tearing shield destroyed one main solar panel and jammed the other under metal debris, leaving the space station underpowered and rapidly overheating to over 130 degrees Fahrenheit. The high heat threatened to release toxic gases and ruin onboard electronics. Eleven days later, astronauts Charles Conrad, Paul Weitz, and Joseph Kerwin launched aboard Skylab 2 to attempt space's first major orbital repair. Working from inside, they pushed a parasol sunshade out through an instrument port, dropping temperatures back to livable levels. Then, during a risky spacewalk, Conrad and Kerwin cut the metal debris jamming the remaining solar panel. When the panel snapped open, the recoil flung both astronauts cartwheeling into space, saved only by their safety tethers. Power surged back on, saving the space station.
angle: When astronauts forced open Skylab's jammed solar array during an emergency space repair, the sudden recoil catapulted both spacewalkers into the void of space, saved only by their safety tethers.

claims.claim: Skylab was launched into Earth orbit on May 14, 1973, aboard a modified Saturn V rocket.
Aerodynamic forces during launch tore off Skylab's micrometeoroid shield, which also functioned as its thermal shield.
The loss of the micrometeoroid shield completely ripped away one of the station's main solar array panels.
Debris from the lost shield jammed Skylab's remaining main solar panel, preventing it from deploying.
Without the thermal shield, internal temperatures aboard Skylab rose to over 130 degrees Fahrenheit, threatening to release toxic gases and ruin equipment.
The damage to both main solar panels left the space station with a severe electrical power deficit.
The first crewed repair mission, Skylab 2, launched on May 25, 1973, carrying astronauts Charles Conrad, Paul Weitz, and Joseph Kerwin.
To lower temperatures, the crew deployed a replacement parasol sunshade through an airlock instrument port from inside the station.
Deploying the parasol sunshade brought Skylab's internal temperatures down to acceptable, livable levels.
Astronauts Conrad and Kerwin performed a spacewalk using a cutter on a 25-foot pole to sever the metal strap jamming the solar array.
When the jammed solar array beam broke free and opened, the sudden release of tension sent both Conrad and Kerwin tumbling into space until their safety tethers caught them.
Freeing the solar array allowed its solar panels to deploy and begin generating power, saving the space station.
The Skylab 2 crew successfully stayed aboard the repaired space station for 28 days.

disputed: Peak temperature discrepancies: Source S6 mentions internal temperatures reached over 130°F to 150°F, whereas source S5 notes exterior temperatures reached 200°F higher than expected. The script should attribute internal heat generally as exceeding 130°F.

Mission numbering discrepancy: Contemporary 1973 reporting in S7 refers to the final 84-day crewed mission as Skylab 3, whereas main historical sources (S1, S5) label the crewed missions sequentially as Skylab 2, Skylab 3, and Skylab 4. The script should use standard mission names or reference crews by astronaut names.
